581.t: Roy Eldridge's love of playing: 'I'm here'
581.s: Eldridge plays hard in an empty room, stuns Locke on 'Caravan' in Toronto, and presses the wrong valves for the right notes.
581.ch: Metropole and Ryan's with Roy Eldridge
581.q: I’ve never played with anyone that loved to play as much as him. Never. And my greatest story, every time I tell somebody this, they always, they love it, but I’m going to tell this so this will be on film forever. I will never forget, we were playing in a place and there was no one in the place,…

581.t: Eldridge's energy, competitiveness and the Dizzy Gillespie story
581.s: His fitness, building solos, challenging anyone on stage, and Dizzy asking to play alone outside Ryan's.
581.ch: Metropole and Ryan's with Roy Eldridge
581.q: I’ve never seen — that’s when I’m trying to tell you. I’ve never seen, I mean sometimes he would start playing and it would just like — you couldn’t believe that this guy could keep building. That’s another thing they told me about, building a solo. They built a solo. They knew how to build a solo.…

109.t: Roy's embouchure change and his New York trip
109.s: Dance and Clarke discuss Roy's range, his tooth trouble, and how his stay in New York made him a local god.
109.ch: Learning drums and Roy Eldridge's band
109.q: And of course everyone thought, well, Roy's the king, you know, he's been to New York, and Small's Paradise, he's played with all the great musicians.

109.t: Pittsburgh clubs, jamming and Little Louis
109.s: Joining Roy in a Pittsburgh cabaret; Pittsburgh was a tough town for visiting musicians, with trumpeter Little Louis and Roy cutting visitors.
109.ch: Learning drums and Roy Eldridge's band
109.q: Oh, boy. Any musician, they were kind of afraid to come to Pittsburgh, because they could find their -- meet their match there, you know. I don't care what instrument you played, we were always running around and knock on the door of some trumpet player. And Little Louis, we used to call him, say,…

92.t: Roy Eldridge playing trumpet on his back
92.s: At the Three Deuces, Roy would get high and play lying down, apparently just as well.
92.ch: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
92.q: L-a-n-h-a-n. Lanhan. They spelled it wrong there, they put a G in there. You know. But a marvelous teacher. But at this time as I told you I was working at the Three Duces, and was with Roy and it was so exciting there. Roy would get high and lay on his back and play the trumpet. And just anything.

92.t: Roy as world's greatest trumpeter; Dizzy jamming at the Savoy again
92.s: Collins repeats the Paul Whiteman poll story that took Eldridge's band to the Savoy opposite Erskine Hawkins, where only Dizzy would jam with Roy.
92.ch: Looking back: rock, blues, childhood and guitar innovators
92.q: So during that time you had some great trumpet players, and of course Roy at that time was considered the president, as I stated before. Paul Whiteman was writing for (or something) the Saturday Evening Post Company, used to have this jazz poll. And he gave Roy the title of the king of the trumpet…

78.t: Roy Eldridge's records: 'Let Me Off Uptown' and 'After You've Gone'
78.s: Horace praises Roy's work with Krupa and Anita O'Day, and says he played the 'After You've Gone' introduction in Horace's band before Krupa.
78.ch: Portraits from Hemphill to Getz, and the bebop question
78.q: Actually, the phrasing of it, you know. But " little Jazz " -- he could play, you know, and, of course, he did some great things with Gene Krupa and Anita O'Day.

78.t: Hiring Roy Eldridge on his playing, not the Stampede solo story
78.s: Horace denies that he hired Roy for copying Hawkins' Stampede solo; he hired him for his fast, correct playing on tunes like 'I Got Rhythm'.
78.ch: Setting the record straight on Hendersonia
78.q: He might have just had that up his sleeve to play, but it was no big thing made out of it. I hired Roy because the thing that, as I said before, actually sold me on Roy, he could play fast tunes like I Got Rhythm and played the correct things and this is why I hired Roy. Where this information came…

383.t: Roy Eldridge as jam-session leader and a giant of the trumpet
383.s: Wilson praises Roy Eldridge's pure jazz feeling, ranking him after Armstrong.
383.q: Of course, one of the great spearheads of the jam sessions was Roy Eldridge -- he just loved to play, and find these trumpet players and blast them out in these different towns.

86.t: Roy Eldridge in Cleveland and Armstrong's endurance
86.s: McKinney's Cotton Pickers came through, Roy Eldridge jammed after hours, and Edison says only he and Armstrong could play endlessly.
86.ch: Jeter-Pillars in Cleveland and St. Louis
86.q: Yeah, yeah. And then I'll never forget, while in Cleveland, McKinney's Cotton Pickers came through there. They had Roy Eldridge, Billy Bowen, Teddy Wilson, Teddy Wilson's brother Gus. Oh, man, what a band he had. What a band he had. And Clyde Hart was playing in the band. And this was later on,…

473.t: Roy Eldridge's range and habit of jumping on bandstands; Little Jazz
473.s: Roy's range grew later; the two went around sitting in everywhere, with Roy sitting on the chair edge stomping, and he earned the nickname Little Jazz, appreciated more by musicians than the public.
473.ch: Horace Henderson band and Roy Eldridge
473.q: Yeah, he could have. Because when I hear him now he's hitting those high B-Flats and things. At that time if he hit a good F -- if he hit a good F back in them days that was a high note, you know.
